newsitem.title: CHINA: China to fight bankruptcy abuse - central banker.
newsitem.headline: China to fight bankruptcy abuse - central banker.

text.p: China will fight illegal bankruptcies to avoid wasting government funds and damaging the nation's credit system, central bank governor Dai Xianglong said on Friday.

Firms applying for bankruptcy would have to seek approval from the main creditor bank before being declared exempt from repaying bank loans, the Xinhua news agency quoted Dai, governor of the People's Bank of China, as saying.
The banking system could be seriously harmed if enterprises were allowed to avoid repaying bank loans by declaring themselves bankrupt, Dai said.

China has many ailing state enterprises that are losing money and unable to repay loans. About 75 percent of its more than 100,000 state firms lost money last year and total losses in the government sector soared to 69 billion yuan ($8.3 billion) between January and October, a year-on-year rise of 45 percent.
China has a bankruptcy law but it is reluctant to use it to avoid widespread layoffs that might create social unrest.
Banks are particularly wary of forcing firms into bankruptcy as they are often unable to protect their claims to assets of a bankrupt firm.
More state enterprises would be merged or declared bankrupt in 1997 and state-owned commercial banks would grant more financial support for such firms, Dai said.
The banks would spend "a fairly large amount of reserve funds to write off bad debts from bankrupt enterprises," he said without elaborating.
China has said it will write off up to 30 billion yuan ($3.6 billion) of bad debt this year and says this figure could rise gradually in the next few years.
Vice-premier and economic tsar Zhu Rongji said on Thursday China should push ahead with reform of state firms this year and force through layoffs and bankruptcies to halt mounting losses.
